source_text: Nunc ad diuina testimonia transeamus. sed prius unum proferam, quod est simile diuino et ob nimiam uetustatem et quod is quem nominabo ex hominibus in deos relatus est.. apud Ciceronem U. Cotta pontifex disputans contra Stoicos de religionibus et uarietate opinionum quae solent esse de diis, ut more Academicorum omnia faceret incerta, quinque fuisse Mercurios ait et enumeratis per ordinem quattuor quintum fuisse eum a quo sit Argus occisus; ob eamque causam in Aegyptum profugisse atque Aegyptiis leges ac litteras tradidisse. hunc Aegyptii Thoyth appellant, a quo apud eos primus anni sui mensis id est September nomen accepit. idem oppidum condidit, quod etiam nunc graece uocatur Mercurii ciuitas, et Pheneatae colunt eum religiose. qui tametsi homo fuit, antiquissimus tamen et instructissimus omni genere doctrinae adeo, ut ei multarum rerum et artium scientia Trismegisto cognomen inponeret. hic scripsit libros et quidem multos ad cognitionem diuinarum rerum pertinentes, in quibus maiestatem summi ac singularis dei asserit isdemque nominibus appellat quibus nos dominum et patrem. ac ne quis nomen eius requireret, άνώνυμον esse dixit, eo quod nominis proprietate non egeat, ob ipsam scilicet unitatem. ipsius haec uerba sunt: o se Oso; είς, b δὲ είς όνόματος ou προσδέεται έστι ykp o wv ὰνώνυμος. deo igitur nomen (non) est, quia solus est, nec opus est proprio uocabulo, nisi cum discrimen exigit multitudo, ut unam quamque personam sua nota et appellatione designes. deo autem, quia semper unus est, proprium nomen est deus. Superest de responsis sacrisque carminibus testimonia quae sunt multo certiora proferre. nam fortasse ii contra quos agimus nec poetis putent esse credendum tamquam uana fingentibus nec philosophis, quod errare potuerint, quia et ipsi homines fuerint. M. Varro, quo nemo umquam doctior ne apud Graecos quidem uixit, in libris rerum diuinarum quos ad C. Caesarem pontificem maximum scripsit, cum de quindecimuiris loqueretur, Sibyllinos libros ait non fuisse unius Sibyllae, sed appellari uno nomine Sibyllinos, quod omnes feminae uates Sibyllae sint a ueteribus nuncupatae uel ab unius Delphidis nomine uel a consiliis deorum enuntiandis. atouq enim deos, non Osouc, et consilium non βουλήν, sed βούλλαν appellabant Aeolico genere sermonis. itaque Sibyllam dictam esse quasi θεοβούλην. ceterum Sibyllas decem numero fuisse, easque omnes enumerauit sub auctoribus qui de singulis scriptitauerint. primam fuisse de Persis, cuius mentionem fecerit Nicanor, qui res gestas Alexandri Macedonis scripsit; secundam Libyssam, cuius meminerit Euripides in Lamiae prologo; tertiam Delphida, de qua Chrysippus loquatur in eo libro quem de diuinatione conposuit; quartam Cimmeriam in Italia, quam Naeuius in libris belli Punici, Piso in annalibus nominet; quintam Erythraeam, quam Apollodorus Erythraeus adfirmet suam fuisse ciuem eamque Grais Ilium petentibus uaticinatam et perituram esse Troiam et Homerum mendacia scripturum; sextam Samiam, de qua scribat Eratosthenes in antiquis annalibus Samiorum repperisse so scriptum; septimam Cumanam nomine Amaltheam, quae ab aliis Herophile uel Demophile nominetur, eamque nouem libros attulisse ad regem Tarquinium Priscum ac pro iis trecentos philippeos postulasse regemque aspernatum pretii magnitudinem derisisse mulieris insaniam; illam in conspectu regis tris combussisse ac pro reliquis idem pretium poposcisse; Tarquinium multo magis insanire mulierem putauisse; quae denuo tribus aliis exustis cum in eodem pretio perseueraret, motum esse regem ac residuos trecentis aureis emisse; quorum postea numerus sit auctus, Capitolio refecto, quod ex omnibus ciuitatibus et Italicis et Graecis praecipueque Erythraeis coacti adlatique sunt Romam cuiuscumque Sibyllae nomine fuerunt; octauam Hellespontiam in agro Troiano natam, uico Marmesso circa oppidum Gergithium, quam scribat Heraclides Ponticus Solonis et Cyri fuisse temporibus; nonam Phrygiam, quae uaticinata sit Ancyrae; decimam Tiburtem nomine Albuneam, quae Tiburi colatur ut dea iuxta ripas amnis Anienis, cuius in gurgite simulacrum eius inuentum esse dicitur tenens in manu librum. arum onmium Sibyllarum carmina et teruntur et habentur, praeterquam Cymaeae, cuius libri a Romanis occultantur nec eos ab ullo nisi a quindecimuiris inspici fas habent. et sunt singularum singuli libri: quos, quia Sibyllae nomine inscribuntur, unius esse credunt, suntque confusi nec discerni ac suum cuique adsignari potest nisi Erythraeae, quae et nomen suum uerum carmini inseruit et Erythraeam se nominatuiri praelocuta est, cum esset orta Babylone. sed et IlOS confuse Sibyllam dicemus, sicubi testimoniis earum ruent abutendum. omnes igitur hae Sibyllae unum deum praedicant, maxime tamen Erythraea, quae celebrior inter ceteras ac nobilior habetur, siquidem Fenestella diligentissimus scriptor de quindecim uiris dicens ait restituto Capitolio rettulisse ad senatum C. Curionem consulem, ut legati Erythras mitterentur, qui carmina Sibyllae conquisita Romam deportarent: itaque missos esse P. Gabinium M. Otacilium L. Valerium, qui descriptos a priuatis uersus circa mille Romam deportarunt. idem dixisse Varronem supra ostendimus. in his ergo uersibus quos Romam legati adtulerunt de uno deo haec sunt testimonia: εἷς θεός, ὂς μόνος ἄρχει, ὐπερμεγέθης ἀγένητος. hunc esse solum summum deum, qui caelum fecerit luminibusque distinxerit: ἀλλὰ θεὸς μόνος εἶς πανυπέρτατος, ὃς πεποίηκεν οὐρανὸν ἡέλιὸν τε καὶ ἀστέρας, ἠδέ σελήνην, καρποφόρον γαῖαν τε καὶ ὕδατος οἴδματα πόντου. qui quoniam solus sit aedificator mundi et artifex rerum uel quibus constat uel quae in eo sunt, solum coli oportere testatur: αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον ὄντα σέβεσθ᾽ ἡγήτορα κόσμου. ὃς μόνος εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ἐτύχθη. item alia Sibylla quaecumque est cum perferre se ad homines uocem dei diceret, sic ait: μοῦνος γὰρ θεὸς εἰμὶ καὶ οὐκ ἔστι θεὸς ἄλλος. Exequerer nunc testimonia ceterarum, nisi et haec sufticerent et illa opportunioribus locis reseruarem. sed cum defendamus causam ueritatis aput eos qui aberrantes a ueritate falsis religionibus seruiunt, quod genus probationis aduersus eos magis adhibere debemus quam ut eos deorum suorum testimoniis reuincamus?
pass_a_gloss: Now let us proceed to divine testimonies. But first I will bring forth one thing which is similar to the divine and because of its great antiquity and because the one whom I will name was transferred from men into gods. In Cicero, Cotta the pontifex, disputing against the Stoics about religions and the variety of opinions which are accustomed to be about gods, so that, in the manner of the Academics, he might make all things uncertain, says that there were five Mercurys and, having enumerated four in order, the fifth was the one by whom Argus was killed; and on account of this cause he fled into Egypt and handed over laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call this one Thoyth, from whom among them the first month of the year, that is September, received its name. The same one founded a city, which is even now called the city of Mercury in Greek, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Who, although he was a man, was nevertheless most ancient and most instructed in every kind of doctrine, so much so that the knowledge of many things and arts gave him the surname Trismegistus. This one wrote books, and indeed many, pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and calls him by the same names by which we call the Lord and Father. And lest anyone might seek his name, he said that it is anonymous, because it does not need the property of a name, on account of its unity. These are his words: O the one Osos; one, and not one of a name, but the one who is anonymous. Therefore, God does not have a name, because he is alone, nor is a proper word needed, except when a multitude demands a distinction, so that you might designate each person by their own mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, the proper name is God. It remains to bring forth testimonies which are much more certain from the sacred and Sibylline poems. For perhaps those against whom we are arguing do not think that poets should be believed, as if they were inventing vain things, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, since they also were men. M. Varro, than whom no one was ever more learned, not even among the Greeks, in the books of divine things which he wrote to C. Caesar the pontifex maximus, when he was speaking about the quindecimvirs, says that the Sibylline books were not of one Sibyl, but are called by one name Sibylline, because all women who are seers are called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the counsels of the gods being announced. For the Aeolians called the gods not Osouc, but theos, and counsel not βουλήν, but βούλλαν. And so the Sibyl is said to be as if θεοβούλην. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and he enumerated all of them under the authors who wrote about each one. The first was from Persia, whom Nicanor mentioned, who wrote about the deeds of Alexander the Macedonian; the second was Libyssa, whom Euripides remembered in the prologue of Lamia; the third was Delphid, about whom Chrysippus spoke in that book which he composed about divination; the fourth was Cimmerian in Italy, whom Naevius named in the books of the Punic war, and Piso in the annals; the fifth was Erythraean, whom Apollodorus the Erythraean affirmed to be his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks who were going to Ilium that Troy would be destroyed and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was Samian, about whom Eratosthenes wrote in the ancient annals of the Samians, having found it written; the seventh was Cuman, named Amalthea, who was also called Herophile or Demophile by others, and who brought nine books to king Tarquin the Elder and demanded three hundred philippeos for them, and the king, having scorned the magnitude of the price, derided the woman's insanity; she, having burned three of them in the sight of the king, demanded the same price for the remaining ones; Tarquin, thinking that the woman was much more insane, was moved, and bought the remaining ones for three hundred gold pieces; the number of which was later increased, the Capitol having been rebuilt, which was brought and gathered from all the cities, both Italian and Greek, and especially Erythraean, to Rome, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were; the eighth was Hellespontian, born in the Trojan field, in the village Marmesso, near the city Gergithium, whom Heraclides Ponticus wrote was in the time of Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was Phrygian, who prophesied in Ancyra; the tenth was Tiburtine, named Albunea, who is worshiped as a goddess in Tibur, near the banks of the river Anienus, whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool, holding a book in her hand. And the poems of all the Sibyls are both corrupted and preserved, except for those of the Cumaean, whose books are hidden by the Romans, and it is not lawful for anyone to inspect them except the quindecimvirs. And there are individual books of each one: which, because they are inscribed with the name of the Sibyl, are believed to be of one, and are confused, nor can they be discerned and assigned to each one, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into the poem and proclaimed that she was called Erythraean, since she was born in Babylon. But also we will call the Sibyl confusedly, wherever we will use their testimonies. Therefore, all these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is considered more famous and noble among the others, since Fenestella, a most diligent writer, saying that the quindecimvirs restored the Capitol, reported to the senate that the consul C. Curio sent legates to Erythrae, who brought back the poems of the Sibyl to Rome: and so legates were sent, P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, L. Valerius, who brought back to Rome about a thousand verses written by private individuals. The same Varro said above. In these verses, which the legates brought back to Rome, there are these testimonies about one God: One God, who alone rules, immense, unborn. That this one is the only highest God, who made the heaven and distinguished it with lights: But God alone is one, most high, who made the heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waves of the sea. Who, since he is alone the builder of the world and the artisan of things, either which consist in it or which are in it, testifies that he alone should be worshiped: This one, who is the only ruler of the world, should be revered. Who alone is from eternity and to eternity. Also, another Sibyl, whoever she is, when she says that she brings the voice of God to men, says thus: For I am the only God, and there is no other God. I would now bring forth the testimonies of the other Sibyls, if these were not sufficient and if I were reserving them for more opportune places. But since we are defending the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof ought we to use against them more than to convict them by the testimonies of their own gods?
pass_b_english: Let us now turn to the divine testimonies. But first I shall bring forward one thing that resembles the divine, both on account of its great antiquity and because the man I shall name was reckoned among the gods. In Cicero the pontifex Cotta, disputing against the Stoics about religions and the variety of opinions customary about the gods, and doing so in the manner of the Academics so that he might render all things uncertain, says there were five Mercuries. After enumerating four in order, he states that the fifth was the one by whom Argus was killed; on that account he fled to Egypt and delivered laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call this figure Thoyth, from whom their first month of the year, September, took its name. He also founded a city that is still called in Greek the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Although he was a man, he was the most ancient and the most thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many matters and arts earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and calls him by the same names by which we call the Lord and Father. Lest anyone seek his name, he declared that he is anonymous, because he does not need the property of a name, on account of his very unity. His words are these: "O the One, Osos; one, and the one does not need a name, for he is anonymous." Therefore God has no name, because he is alone, nor is a proper word required, except when a multitude demands a distinction, so that you may designate each person by his own mark and appellation. But for God, since he is always one, the proper name is God.

It remains to produce testimonies from the sacred and Sibylline poems, which are much more certain. For perhaps those against whom we argue do not think poets should be believed, as if they invent vain things, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, since they too were men. Marcus Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived, not even among the Greeks, in the books on divine matters which he wrote to Gaius Caesar the pontifex maximus, when speaking of the quindecimvirs, says the Sibylline books were not the work of one Sibyl, but are called by the single name Sibylline because all women seers were named Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For the Aeolians called the gods not Osouc but theos, and counsel not boule but bulla; and so the Sibyl is said to be, as it were, theoboule. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and he enumerated them all under the authors who wrote about each one. The first was from Persia, whom Nicanor mentioned, who wrote the deeds of Alexander the Macedonian; the second was the Libyan, whom Euripides remembered in the prologue of the Lamia; the third was the Delphic, about whom Chrysippus spoke in the book he composed on divination; the fourth was the Cimmerian in Italy, whom Naevius named in the books of the Punic War and Piso in the annals; the fifth was the Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirmed to be his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks sailing for Ilium that Troy would be destroyed and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was the Samian, about whom Eratosthenes wrote in the ancient annals of the Samians, having found it written; the seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea, who was also called Herophile or Demophile by others, and who brought nine books to King Tarquin the Elder and demanded three hundred philippeos for them, whereupon the king scorned the magnitude of the price and derided the woman's insanity; she burned three of them in the king's sight and demanded the same price for the remaining ones; Tarquin thought the woman all the more insane, yet was moved and bought the remaining ones for three hundred gold pieces; the number of which was later increased when the Capitol was rebuilt, for books were collected and brought to Rome from all cities, both Italian and Greek, and especially from Erythrae, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were; the eighth was the Hellespontian, born in the Trojan territory, in the village of Marmessus near the city of Gergithus, whom Heraclides Ponticus wrote lived in the times of Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra; the tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea, who is worshipped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the river Anio, whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The poems of all the Sibyls are both worn and preserved, except for those of the Cumaean, whose books are hidden by the Romans, and it is not lawful for anyone to inspect them except the quindecimvirs. And there are individual books of each one: which, because they are inscribed with the name of the Sibyl, are believed to be of one, and are confused, nor can they be discerned and assigned to each one, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into the poem and proclaimed that she was called Erythraean, since she was born in Babylon. Therefore all these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is considered more famous and noble among the rest, since Fenestella, a most diligent writer, saying that the quindecimvirs restored the Capitol, reported to the senate that the consul Gaius Curio sent legates to Erythrae, who brought back the poems of the Sibyl to Rome; and so legates were sent, Publius Gabinius, Marcus Otacilius, Lucius Valerius, who brought back to Rome about a thousand verses copied from private individuals. Who, since he is alone the builder of the world and the artisan of things, either which consist in it or which are in it, testifies that he alone should be worshipped: This one, who is the only ruler of the world, should be revered. Who alone is from eternity and to eternity." Also another Sibyl, whoever she is, when she says that she brings the voice of God to men, says thus: "For I am the only God, and there is no other God."
